ol96b1-bb9927.summary: Auriol's question whether the theological habit is practical or speculative, prompted by Lombard's statement that his aim is to overturn heretics and defend the faith. Five sets of initial arguments make theology purely speculative, purely practical, chiefly speculative and qualifiedly practical, simply both, or affective and loving; the contrary arguments deny any practical character. Article 1 reviews twelve opinions in four families and rejects them: the purely speculative views (Henry and others), Ware's supernatural-prudence view and the 'virtues joined to works' view, Scotus's restriction of praxis to the will, Godfrey's two habits, Thomas's 'simply speculative, qualifiedly practical' (dividing differences cannot so combine), and the affective, amative and contemplative views of Giles of Rome, John of Paris and others. Article 2 reworks the concept of the practical against Scotus: praxis can be intellectual (logic and rhetoric are practical, and logic's subject is expressive discourse), practicality consists formally in activity, it derives from the object as operable by the knower, and speculative and practical essentially divide science as an intellectual virtue. Article 3 concludes that theology is purely practical, directing belief immediately and love finally; that it resides in the speculative intellect, as a universal practical habit; and that it is nobler than any speculative science and than it would be if speculative.
claims: Theology is a purely practical habit whose end includes the acts of faith and charity it directs.
A habit is practical formally by its activity toward an object operable by the knower.
Praxis can be an act within the intellect; logic and rhetoric are practical.
Speculative and practical are essential differences of science considered as intellectual virtue.
Theology resides in the speculative intellect though practical.
Theology is nobler than any speculative science.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e107.summary: Title of the question: whether the theological habit is practical or speculative.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e114.summary: Ties the question to Lombard's prologue, which suggests that theology's end is to overthrow heretics and defend the faith, and so raises the question of theology's end: is it purely practical or speculative? First argument for purely speculative: a merely declarative habit that is wisdom seems purely speculative, since wisdom is in the speculative intellect (Ethics VI), and the previous question showed theology is such a habit.
claims: (Argument) Wisdom belongs to the speculative intellect.
(Argument) A declarative habit that is wisdom is speculative.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e154.summary: Argues that no acquired science is nobler than theology, speculative science is nobler than practical (Metaphysics I), and some acquired sciences (geometry, physics) are purely speculative, so theology must be speculative.
claims: (Argument) Speculative science is nobler than practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e170.summary: Argues that a habit whose end is speculation is speculative, and theology's end is speculation. Augustine says all our work in this life is to heal the eye of the heart so that God may be seen, and speculation is better than action, the contemplative life better than the active.
claims: (Argument) The end of theology is the vision of God.
(Argument) Contemplation is better than action.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e196.summary: Rubric introducing arguments that theology is purely practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e201.summary: Argues that theology is purely practical. The end of a practical habit is knowing how to act, not acting: prudence's end is knowing how to act, while the moral virtues elicit the act, and a habit's end is the operation it elicits, in its own power, so for intellectual habits it is knowing. Theology's end is knowing how to act so as to reach eternal life.
claims: (Argument) The end of a practical habit is knowing how to act, not the act itself.
(Argument) Theology's end is knowing how to act for eternal life.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e240.summary: Argues that a habit whose end is operations is practical. Charity and other virtues are theology's end ('the end of the precept is charity'; Augustine), but chiefly as joined to works: so they unite most with the last end, are infused for works, are most perfect, and form the one way to eternal life. So theology is purely practical.
claims: (Argument) The virtues are theology's end chiefly as joined to works.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e277.summary: Rubric introducing arguments that theology is practical in a qualified sense and speculative simply.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e285.summary: Argues that theology, being a higher, more common single habit, extends to the matters of the various philosophical sciences under the common character of being knowable by divine light. Since philosophy divides into speculative and practical with the speculative principal, theology is both but chiefly speculative. Confirmed: God knows himself and his works by one science, more speculative than practical.
claims: (Argument) Theology is one higher habit embracing speculative and practical matters, but chiefly speculative.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e322.summary: Argues that a habit that considers human acts but orders them to perfect knowledge of God is practical in considering morals but more speculative, since it orders them to knowing and contemplating God. Theology is such a habit.
claims: (Argument) Theology orders human acts to the knowledge of God.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e340.summary: Rubric introducing arguments that theology is simply practical and simply speculative.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e347.summary: Argues that theology treats morals more perfectly than moral philosophy and God and separate substances more perfectly than metaphysics. So it is simply practical where it is moral and simply speculative where it treats divine things.
claims: (Argument) Theology treats morals better than ethics and divine things better than metaphysics.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e382.summary: Argues from Augustine's distinction of wisdom (about eternal reasons, purely speculable) and science (about administering temporal things). Theology is both, so it is simply practical and simply speculative.
claims: (Argument) Theology is both wisdom and science in Augustine's sense.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e404.summary: Rubric introducing arguments that theology is affective and loving.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e410.summary: Argues that theology is affective. A habit whose end is affection and love is neither speculative (end: speculating) nor practical (end: operating), and Augustine (De doctrina christiana I) says the end and fullness of Scripture is love, as many canonical and patristic texts confirm.
claims: (Argument) The end of Scripture is love.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e432.summary: Argues that the best habit in this life should have the best end, and charity is best in this life. Understanding is simply nobler than willing, but charitable willing is more useful, as bread is more useful than a mouse though the mouse is nobler, and philosophizing is better than getting rich, but not for the needy (Topics III). So charity is theology's end, and theology is affective.
claims: (Argument) Charitable willing is more useful in this life than understanding.
(Argument) Charity is the end of theology.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e467.summary: Rubric introducing arguments that theology is in no way practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e474.summary: Argues that a habit sought for its own sake and to escape ignorance is not practical, affective or ordered to love. Theology is more for its own sake than metaphysics and revealed to escape ignorance, and it does not increase love, since simple believers sometimes love more than theologians.
claims: (Argument) Theology does not increase love.
(Argument) Theology is sought for its own sake.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e503.summary: Argues that theology relates to supernatural love as natural sciences relate to natural love. No natural science (metaphysics, mathematics) is ordered to natural love, so theology is not ordered to supernatural love.
claims: (Argument) Natural sciences are not ordered to natural love.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e525.summary: Rubric marking the response to the question.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e531.summary: Lays out the response: first twelve opinions of the doctors, then how 'speculative' and 'practical' relate to science, then Auriol's own answer.

ol96b1-bb9927-Dd1e547.summary: Surveys and refutes the doctors' opinions on whether theology is practical or speculative, arranged by the four combinations (purely speculative, purely practical, both, neither). Against the speculative views (Henry; those making love the end yet calling theology speculative; those limiting praxis to external works): the end of theology in this life is charity and the virtues, God is 'operable' through our acts, and directing the will is practical, as prudence shows. Against the practical views: Ware's 'knowing how to act' mistakes the end of practical habits, which is the operation itself; the view that virtues are ends as joined to works inverts love and works; Scotus rightly ties praxis to the will but wrongly excludes acts of intellect. Against the 'both' views: Godfrey's two habits break the unity that faith and Scripture show; Thomas's 'simply speculative, qualifiedly practical' combines dividing differences incoherently, and its inverse fares no better. Against the 'neither' views (affective, amative, contemplative): every intellectual habit is practical or speculative, and habits ordered to love or affection, like ethics and prudence, are practical.
claims: Theology's end in this life is charity, faith and the virtues, not speculation.
The end of a practical habit is the operation it directs, not knowing how to act.
A habit ordered to an operation elicited by another habit, in will or intellect, is practical.
Theology is a single habit.
Speculative and practical cannot combine in one habit with one simple and one qualified.
Every intellectual habit is either practical or speculative.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e556.summary: Notes that 'speculative' and 'practical' can be combined in four ways with respect to a habit, along which the doctors divide.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e567.summary: Lists the four combinations: purely speculative, purely practical, both, or neither.
claims: A habit can be purely speculative, purely practical, both, or neither.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e583.summary: Rubric naming Henry of Ghent's opinion (Summa a. 8, q. 3) as the first examined.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e589.summary: Those who call theology purely speculative divide three ways. The first say its end is mere speculation, supported by the first three arguments. Auriol replies: if this is speculation in this life, it contradicts the saints, who order theology to charity, faith, hope and the virtues. If it is the speculation of heaven, that does not make the habit speculative, since all sciences are finally ordered to beatitude (Avicenna) yet not all are speculative, and only a speculation elicited by the habit makes it speculative. Otherwise ethics, which disposes to speculation (Averroes: chastity aids knowledge), would be speculative. Heavenly vision is not elicited by theology.
claims: (Reported) Theology is speculative because its end is speculation.
The saints order theology to charity and the virtues, not to speculation in this life.
Only a speculation elicited by a habit makes that habit speculative.
All sciences are ultimately ordered to beatitude without all being speculative.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e654.summary: Rubric for the opinion that theology is speculative even though love is its end.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e661.summary: Second speculative view: love is theology's end (following the saints), but since love is an act of will toward the last end, which is not something to be done, theology remains speculative. Auriol replies that God is attainable by us through acts of intellect and will, and since one can err in such acts they need a directing habit, which is practical.
claims: (Reported) Love of God as end does not make theology practical, since God is not operable.
God is 'operable' as attainable through our acts of intellect and will.
Acts in which one can err need a directing, practical habit.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e690.summary: Rubric for the opinion that theology is speculative though it has an act of will as its end.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e697.summary: Third speculative view: only habits directing external works are practical, not those directing acts of will. Auriol replies that prudence is practical because it makes right choice, directing the will, not because it acts externally, and Aristotle calls the mind that moves through the end, for whose sake there is will, practical. If theology moves to and directs charity it is not speculative. To the objection that every speculative habit causes love: that love is not intended as the habit's end, whereas theology is ordered to love by intent.
claims: (Reported) Only habits directing external works are practical.
Prudence is practical because it directs the will's choice.
A habit intentionally ordered to directing love is practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e741.summary: Rubric naming the opinion of Varro (William of Ware), Sentences I q. 1, that theology is practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e749.summary: States Ware's view: theology's end is knowing how to act, true knowledge in harmony with right appetite toward the supernatural good. As prudence relates to all moral virtues, theology is a supernatural prudence directing the theological and infused moral virtues, so it is practical. Auriol rejects its basis, that a practical habit's end is knowing how to act rather than acting. Aristotle says ethics aims not at knowledge but action, we inquire into virtue to become good, and the end of practical science is the work (Metaphysics II). When a habit is the principle of two operations, the more powerful is its end. A practical habit elicits knowing how to act and directs external action, and the latter is more powerful. (The end of the text is corrupt.)
claims: (Reported) Theology is a supernatural prudence whose end is knowledge in harmony with right appetite.
The end of a practical habit is the operation, not knowing how to operate.
A habit's end is the more powerful of the operations it principles.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e856.summary: Rubric naming the opinion attributed to 'Henricus Anglicus' (Summa q. 3 a. B).

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e863.summary: States the view that theology is practical because the virtues are its ends as joined to works, supported by the first of the second group of arguments. Auriol rejects it. Charity and the act of love are most perfect in themselves and intended by Scripture for their own sake; works are for love, not love for works, so love taken purely has the character of last end. Belief, even unjoined to any work, is also theology's end (Augustine: faith is begotten, defended, strengthened). Faith and charity are intended in themselves, not as issuing in external works.
claims: (Reported) Theology is practical because it aims at virtues joined to works.
Charity is intended for its own sake, and works are for love.
Belief itself, apart from works, is an end of theology.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e912.summary: Rubric naming Scotus's opinion (Ordinatio prologue q. 4 and 5): theology is practical because the first praxis is the act of will.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e921.summary: States Scotus's view: love taken absolutely is the end, yet theology is practical, because the first praxis that practical knowledge extends to directing is the act of will; external acts of other powers are praxis only secondarily. Auriol agrees that extension to an act of will makes the intellect practical, but denies that only acts of will are first praxis. An act of intellect can be too, or logic would not be practical (shown later), nor theology insofar as it nourishes belief. Universally, a habit is practical if it is ordered to an operation it does not itself elicit, which some other habit elicits, in any power.
claims: (Reported) The first praxis is the act of will.
Acts of intellect can also be praxis.
A habit is practical when it is ordered to an operation elicited by another habit.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e973.summary: Rubric naming Godfrey of Fontaines' opinion (Quodlibet IX q. 1).

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e979.summary: Those who call theology both practical and speculative divide three ways. Godfrey makes it two habits: a moral, practical one about virtues, vices and precepts, and a speculative one about the Trinity and emanations, supported by the fourth group of arguments. Auriol rejects this. Faith, the adhesive habit toward all of Scripture, moral and speculative, is one habit, so theology, its declarative counterpart, is one. One course of study should not produce two habits. And Scripture would not mix moral and speculative matter within one chapter, sometimes within three lines, if it meant to generate two habits.
claims: (Reported) Theology comprises two habits, one practical and one speculative.
Theology is a single habit, as faith is.
Scripture's interweaving of moral and speculative matter shows the unity of the theological habit.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1034.summary: Rubric naming Thomas Aquinas's opinion (Summa theologiae I q. 1 a. 4).

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1039.summary: States Thomas's view: theology is one habit, practical in a qualified sense and speculative simply, supported by the third group of arguments. Auriol replies that two dividing differences cannot belong to one species with one qualified and one simple, as 'rational' and 'irrational' cannot so combine in one animal. Practical and speculative divide science (Metaphysics VI), so no one habit is qualifiedly practical and simply speculative; claiming both unity and this mixture is contradictory.
claims: (Reported) Theology is one habit, simply speculative and qualifiedly practical.
Dividing differences of a genus cannot combine in one species, even with qualification.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1096.summary: Further objection to Thomas: when extreme differences meet in an intermediate, neither belongs simply, as red is neither simply dispersive (white) nor simply gathering (black) of sight, though nearer black. If theology is a mixture of speculative and practical, it is formally neither, so calling it formally speculative and also mixed is contradictory.
claims: An intermediate mixed from extremes is formally neither extreme.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1138.summary: Further objection to Thomas: a habit that treats human acts as ordered to speculation is wholly speculative, just as ethics, which treats speculable things (parts of the soul, the will's object) ordered to morals, is wholly practical. If theology treats human acts only for the sake of knowledge, it is wholly speculative, against Thomas's view.
claims: A habit is wholly practical or speculative according to the order of its whole consideration.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1169.summary: Rubric for the opinion that theology is simply practical and qualifiedly speculative.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1177.summary: Rejects the opposite view, simply practical and qualifiedly speculative, for the same reasons. The same could be said of any practical science, since every practical science speculates and considers (the Ethics treats much that is speculable), yet such a science is simply practical and in no way speculative.
claims: Every practical science involves consideration without thereby being speculative.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1201.summary: Rubric naming the opinions of Giles of Rome (affective), John of Paris (amative) and others (contemplative).

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1214.summary: Those who say theology is neither practical nor speculative divide three ways: affective (it affects the will), amative (it is ordered to love and charity), or contemplative (contemplation is intellect with the will's delight). All three wrongly posit an intellectual habit outside the division into practical and speculative, against Aristotle.
claims: (Reported) Theology is affective, amative, or contemplative.
Every intellectual habit is either practical or speculative.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1249.summary: Further objection: Aristotle treats friendship in the Ethics yet never calls the habit generated by studying it affective, contemplative or amative, only practical. So theology remains practical even if ordered to affection and charity.
claims: Habits ordered to love are practical, as Aristotle's ethics of friendship shows.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1267.summary: Further objection: prudence is practical, and it and its act are ordered first and per se to right affection, works being made right by rectifying affection. So a habit ordered to affection can be called practical. This ends the survey of opinions.
claims: Prudence is ordered primarily to right affection.
A habit ordered to affection can be practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-Dd1e1284.summary: Analyzes what 'practical' means, against Scotus. Scotus defines praxis as an operation of a power other than intellect, posterior to and conformable to right reason; he makes volition the first praxis even without external acts, places practicality in aptitudinal relations of priority and conformity, treats speculative and practical as proper attributes rather than essential differences, takes practicality from the object rather than the end, and concludes theology is properly practical. Auriol corrects him on four points. Praxis can lie within the intellect: logic and rhetoric are practical, since they direct and even make their objects (expressive discourse in its species) and divide into docens and utens. A habit is practical formally by its activity, not by priority and conformity (Aristotle's equation of practical and active, the rose expert without power, Platonic Ideas, angelic versus human moral science). Practicality comes from the object as operable by the knower, not the object alone. And speculative and practical are essential differences of science considered as an intellectual virtue fitting a knower, though not of science as an absolute quality; the distinction by ends is consequential.
claims: Praxis can be an act within the intellect, so logic and rhetoric are practical.
A habit is practical formally by its activity.
Practicality comes from the object as operable by the knower.
Speculative and practical are essential differences of science as intellectual virtue, though not as absolute quality.
Any habit ordered to an act it directs, in any power, is purely practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1293.summary: Heading of the second article: where 'practical' comes from, how practical and speculative relate to science, and the definition of praxis, against Scotus (Ordinatio prologue q. 4 and 5).

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1306.summary: States Scotus's account: a habit is called practical from some praxis, and the first praxis is the act of will. Praxis is defined as an operation of a power other than intellect, naturally posterior to intellection, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason so as to be right. The conditions are explained next.
claims: (Reported) Praxis is an operation of a power other than intellect, posterior to intellection and apt to conform to right reason.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1337.summary: Scotus's case for the first condition (praxis is outside the intellect): Aristotle recognizes only operations remaining in the intellect and those going outside it, and intellect becomes practical by extension beyond itself.
claims: (Reported) The intellect becomes practical by extending to operations outside itself.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1362.summary: Scotus's further case: willing the end and love are in the will, and since one can act rightly or wrongly regarding them, there can be a practical habit directing them. It suffices that the operation be outside the intellect, so every act of will is praxis.
claims: (Reported) Every act of will is praxis.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1384.summary: Scotus's further case: the operation from which all others are called practical is praxis most of all. External operations are practical because they fall under the will's command and so conform to right reason, so the act of will is chiefly praxis. Second condition: praxis is naturally posterior to intellection, since intellect cannot regulate what precedes it.
claims: (Reported) External operations are practical through the will's command.
(Reported) Praxis must be naturally posterior to intellection.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1432.summary: Scotus's further case: vegetative acts are never practical, since they precede intellect and are not subject to its direction. Third condition: right choice follows right reason, and this holds of every act of will, elicited or commanded, so the rectitude of praxis comes from conformity to intellect.
claims: (Reported) Vegetative acts are not praxis.
(Reported) The rectitude of all praxis comes from conformity with intellect.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1467.summary: Scotus's further case from Augustine (the intellect understands for itself and for the others): operations of other powers are apt to be directed by intellect, and these are praxis.
claims: (Reported) Operations apt to be directed by intellect are praxis.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1487.summary: Rubric introducing the conclusions Scotus draws: volition is the first praxis, and others.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1496.summary: Scotus's first inference: the first praxis is the act of will, since commanded acts conform to intellect only through volition, and what first conforms is first praxis.
claims: (Reported) Volition is the first praxis.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1515.summary: Scotus's second inference: volition is praxis even without any commanded act or external work. What is primarily so remains so when separated from what follows, and the intellectual appetite is a moving principle like the sensitive, whose rational motion is praxis.
claims: (Reported) Volition is praxis apart from external acts.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1554.summary: Scotus's third inference: being practical consists in two aptitudinal relations, priority and natural conformity to praxis. They are aptitudinal because a practical habit need not actually be extended to conforming an operation.
claims: (Reported) A practical habit consists in aptitudinal relations of priority and conformity.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1593.summary: Scotus's fourth inference: speculative and practical are not essential differences of science, since no relation is a formal difference of an absolute thing. They are proper attributes, like even and odd for number or straight and curved for lines, so dividing science into them is like dividing a genus by the proper attributes of its species.
claims: (Reported) Speculative and practical are proper attributes of science, not essential differences.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1624.summary: Scotus's fifth inference: being practical comes from the object, not the end, since conformability and posteriority come from the nature of the object (contingent and operable) and from the intellect, whether or not it is set as end. Confirmed: these aptitudes belong to a science through its absolute form, which has them from the object; and the end causes only when loved, while a habit is practical even with nothing actually intended.
claims: (Reported) The practical character of a habit derives from its object, not its end.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1672.summary: Scotus's sixth and main inference: theology is most properly practical. Practical knowledge is apt to conform to right volition and naturally prior to it, and theology is needed for the created intellect to conform to and rectify the love of God, which it precedes. From considering the triune God and other truths we learn what the will's end should be and how and by what ways to tend to it, so theology supplies the principles of rectitude in all our volition. The same holds for theology about contingent things.
claims: (Reported) Theology is properly practical because it rectifies the love of God.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1722.summary: Rubric announcing, against Scotus, that the operation making a habit practical can be in the intellect, and that logic is practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1741.summary: Auriol accepts much of Scotus but denies that praxis must be in a power other than intellect. Logic, rhetoric and all intellectual habits that direct acts elicited in the intellect by another habit are practical. Aristotle calls rhetoric a virtue and Averroes a power and faculty; the same goes for logic, rhetoric being the counterpart of dialectic. A habit with the character of an active power is practical.
claims: Praxis can be an act within the intellect.
Logic and rhetoric are practical habits.
A habit with the character of an active power is practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1787.summary: Further argument: a habit with relations of conformity, priority, activity and direction has more than the character of speculation and is practical. Logic regulates and directs the acts of other sciences and is prior to them, since it is foolish to seek a science and its method together (Metaphysics II).
claims: Logic regulates the acts of other sciences and is prior to them.
Logic is practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1813.summary: Further arguments. A habit whose end is another habit's act is not for its own sake, which speculative habits are (Metaphysics I), and logic aims at directing the acts of other sciences, being introductory. And a habit that extends beyond its own act is practical, since intellect becomes practical by extension, and logic does.
claims: Speculative habits are for their own sake.
Logic is not for its own sake but for directing other sciences.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1850.summary: Further argument: only practical arts divide into teaching and using (as medicine), and logic divides into logica docens and logica utens, so it is practical.
claims: The division into docens and utens marks practical arts.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1863.summary: Further argument: no speculative habit makes its object (astronomy does not make the heavens), while active habits operate on theirs. The logician makes expressive speech (propositions and syllogisms) and the rhetorician persuasive speech. Logic's subject is not the mode of knowing or second intentions but discourse expressive of truth and concepts, in three species: the word (Categories, per Boethius), the proposition (Peri hermeneias), and the syllogism (Prior Analytics generally; demonstrative in the Posterior Analytics, dialectical in the Topics, sophistical in the Sophistical Refutations). Logic makes these, so it is practical. General rule: every habit whose end includes the act it directs, wherever and in whatever power, is truly and purely practical.
claims: Logic's subject is discourse expressive of truth and concepts, not second intentions.
The books of the Organon are distinguished by species of expressive discourse.
Logic makes its objects and is therefore practical.
Any habit ordered to an act it directs, in whatever power, is purely practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1937.summary: Rubric announcing, against Scotus, that a habit is formally practical by its relation of activity, not by relations of priority and conformity.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1951.summary: Argues that a practical habit consists formally in a relation of activity rather than Scotus's two aptitudinal relations. What makes a habit active makes it practical: Aristotle calls practical science 'active' and divides science into speculative and active, and in Greek 'praxis' means action. A habit is active formally through activity.
claims: A habit is formally practical through its activity.
'Practical' and 'active' are the same notion.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1980.summary: Further argument: the practical mind moves (Ethics VI), and the intellect of universals does not move and so is not practical (De anima III). Being practical consists in moving, and so in acting.
claims: Being practical consists in moving and acting.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e1996.summary: Further argument: Aristotle says things come from art, nature or chance, the house in the soul causes the house in matter, and if ship-building were in the wood it would make the ship as it does from the soul. A practical habit is causal and active, and Aristotle mentions no other relation.
claims: Art in the soul is an efficient cause of the artifact.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2020.summary: Further argument: the formal reason of a practical habit is what, once removed, removes practicality while all else remains. Someone with perfect natural science of how roses are generated, able to direct anyone who could produce one, would have priority and conformity, yet not practical physics, since he could not make a rose. So activity alone makes a habit practical.
claims: Priority and conformity without the power to act do not make a habit practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2066.summary: Further argument: if Platonic Ideas subsisted, they would have priority and conformity to things to be made, the artisan working by looking at them, yet they would not be practical, since they would do nothing. So conformity does not make a habit practical; activity does.
claims: Exemplars without activity are not practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2088.summary: Further argument: moral science in an angel's mind is the same species as ours (same object, same kind of power), yet it is not practical in the angel, who cannot acquire chastity, while in us it is. They differ only in activity, both having priority and conformity. Confirmed: if God gave one who knows rose generation the power to execute it, his science would become practical. Auriol rejects two evasions: that activity just is conformability (they are separable, conformity causes direction, and relations differ by foundation and term), and that priority to the product is activity (priority is presupposed but differs from the relation of agent to product). A practical habit is so named not by extrinsic denomination from praxis but from practicing, as 'active' from acting.
claims: Moral science is practical in us but not in angels, though of the same species.
Activity is distinct from conformability and priority.
A habit is practical intrinsically, from its own acting, not by extrinsic denomination.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2185.summary: Rubric announcing, against Scotus, that being practical is not taken from the object alone but from the object related to the knower.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2194.summary: Agrees that speculative and practical come from the object, not the end, but says the object is not enough: habits of the same species and object would then both be practical or both speculative, yet angelic and human moral science are the same species and differ in this.
claims: Practicality comes from the object, but the object alone is insufficient.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2227.summary: Further argument: with the object unchanged, a speculative habit can become practical. Knowledge of rose generation is speculative in us, but if God gave a man the power to make roses (as angels perhaps can by applying actives to passives) it would become practical. Medicine is a kind of physics yet practical because active, and true alchemy would make the physics of metals practical. So practicality belongs to the object as related to a knower with power to produce it, as in Aristotle's definition of practical science (its principle is in the agent, and in artifacts that principle is the will). Practical science concerns what is operable by the knower, speculative science what is only speculable. (The text then becomes corrupt and runs into the next heading: speculative and practical are essential dividing differences of science, against Scotus.)
claims: The same object-knowledge can become practical if power to produce is added.
Practicality belongs to the object as operable by the knower.
Medicine is practical physics because it is active.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2316.summary: Argues against Scotus that speculative and practical are essential differences of science. Aristotle divides science first by them, and species under a difference are essential species of the genus only if the difference divides it essentially (white and black under 'colored' are not species of animal; species under 'irrational' are). Physics, mathematics and metaphysics fall under 'speculative' and are essential species of science, so 'speculative' must be an essential difference.
claims: Speculative and practical are essential differences of science.
Species under a non-essential difference are not species of the genus.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2379.summary: Further argument: what belongs to a habit from its object is essential to it, and practicality comes from the object.
claims: What a habit has from its object is essential to it.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2390.summary: Further argument and resolution. Moral and natural philosophy differ more under science than natural philosophy and metaphysics, which holds only if speculative and practical are essential differences. Resolution: taken in its absolute reality, science is not essentially divided by them (Scotus is right in that sense), since the same habit can be speculative or practical. Taken as an intellectual virtue (Ethics VI), it includes a relation of fittingness to the knower, as virtue in one nature is vice in another. In this sense it is essentially divided, because the intellect relates differently to what is only knowable (reflexive) and to what it can also make (extended toward the work), and the whole mode of teaching, taking principles and knowing differs. Aristotle's distinction by ends is consequential: because the object is operable, the habit is practical and so is ordered to the operation.
claims: As an absolute quality, science is not essentially divided into speculative and practical.
As an intellectual virtue, science is essentially divided by its fittingness to the knower.
Virtue includes a relation of fittingness to the nature that has it.
Distinguishing practical and speculative by ends is consequential, not primary.

ol96b1-bb9927-Dd1e2528.summary: Gives Auriol's answer in three propositions and replies to all the arguments. (1) Theology is purely practical. A priori, its object God is reached more nobly by faith, hope, charity and obedience than by theological declaration. A posteriori, its end includes the act of believing, which it directs but faith elicits; it directs belief most immediately and love most finally. (2) It resides in the speculative, contemplative intellect, not the practical (particular, experiential) intellect, because it reasons from universals; universal habits like logic and moral science can be practical by directing action. (3) It is nobler than any acquired speculative habit, and nobler than if it were speculative, because the acts it directs (loving, believing, hoping in God) surpass declaring, as moral philosophy surpasses geometry. The replies hold that theology is wisdom yet practical, its end being the defense and nourishment of faith and the acts of the theological virtues.
claims: Theology is a purely practical habit.
Theology directs belief immediately and love ultimately.
Theology resides in the speculative intellect though practical.
Theology is nobler than any speculative habit and than it would be if speculative.
Theology is wisdom, not science, and exists for faith and virtue.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2537.summary: Heading of the third article: theology is a purely practical habit.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2542.summary: Announces that Auriol's answer comes in three propositions.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2549.summary: First proposition: theology is a purely practical habit, shown a priori and a posteriori. A priori, from the object as related to the knower: a habit is purely practical if its object can be reached by the knower through nobler operations than the habit's own act, as health is better had than known and virtue better possessed than defined. God is reached more nobly by faith, hope, charity and obedience than by declaring believed things obscurely, so theology is purely practical; that is why theologians deal chiefly with how God is reached through believing, hoping, loving and obeying. A posteriori, from the end: a habit whose end includes an act it directs is purely practical, and theology directs believing, which is elicited by faith, defending, strengthening and generating it (Augustine).
claims: A habit whose object is reachable by nobler operations than its own act is purely practical.
God is reached more nobly by faith, hope, charity and obedience than by theological declaration.
Theology directs the act of believing, which faith elicits.
Theology is a purely practical habit.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2657.summary: Adds that theology directs four acts (believing, hoping, loving and living virtuously, per Augustine). It directs believing most immediately, as declarative of believed things, and loving most finally, as faith is ordered to charity.
claims: Theology directs belief most immediately and love most ultimately.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2686.summary: Rubric announcing the second proposition: theology resides in the speculative intellect.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2693.summary: Second proposition: the theological habit resides not in the deliberative part of the soul (the practical intellect of Ethics VI) but in the speculative, contemplative part with wisdom and science. Habits in the practical intellect are experiential and about particulars, like the empirical physician's, and theology reasons from universals. The practical intellect is particular reason; the speculative intellect is contemplative universal reason. Every operable object can be reached by both, by experience and by deduction, so every science of operables divides into practical (experiential) and theoretical, as in medicine; the experienced often act better than theorists. A habit in the contemplative intellect can still be practical, since 'practical' signifies activity, and one is directed to act both from universals and from particulars.
claims: Theology resides in the speculative or contemplative intellect.
The practical intellect is particular reason, whose habits are experiential.
Every science of operables has an experiential and a theoretical form.
A habit in the contemplative intellect can be practical by directing action from universals.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2834.summary: Rubric announcing the third proposition: theology is nobler than any speculative habit, and nobler than it would be if speculative.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2841.summary: Third proposition: though practical, theology is nobler than any humanly devised speculative habit, since it has the noblest object (God), the noblest elicited act (declaring and defending believed things), and the noblest directed act (faith, hope, love and virtuous living). It is nobler than it would be as speculative: speculative science is generally nobler because it is for its own sake while practical science is ordered to lesser operations, but where the operations are worthier than speculating the practical habit is nobler, and loving, believing and hoping in God are nobler than declaring believed things. Likewise moral philosophy is nobler than geometry, having a better subject and aiming at rectitude of choice, an act of the higher power, the will.
claims: A habit's nobility follows its object, elicited act and directed act.
Theology is nobler than any acquired speculative habit.
A practical habit is nobler than a speculative one when the operations it directs are nobler than speculation.
Moral philosophy is nobler than geometry.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2932.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the first set of arguments.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2938.summary: Replies to the wisdom argument: theology is wisdom and in the speculative intellect yet practical, not in the experiential way of prudence but like logic, moral science and every universal habit directing action, which must be in the contemplative part (Ethics VI).
claims: Theology is wisdom in the speculative intellect and yet practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2962.summary: Replies to the nobility argument: though practical, theology is nobler than any acquired science, as shown.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2971.summary: Replies to the argument from contemplation as end: the speculation theology is ordered to is directed, not elicited, by it, so theology is practical.
claims: Speculation directed by a habit makes it practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2980.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the second set of arguments.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e2991.summary: Replies to the second set: their conclusion is true but the reasons fail. The end of a practical habit is acting, not knowing how to act. Prudence's end is the right choice of the will, which is nobler than knowing. It is false that a habit's end must be an operation it elicits in its own power, since the end is an extrinsic cause. (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: The end of prudence is right choice of the will.
A habit's end need not be an operation it elicits, since the end is an extrinsic cause.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3022.summary: Replies to the second argument: the virtues are not ends through being joined to works; believing, hoping and loving taken in themselves suffice. (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: Believing, hoping and loving are ends in themselves.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3034.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the third set of arguments.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3039.summary: Replies to the first argument of the third set: though theology extends to matters of human speculative and practical sciences, it is only practical, since its end is not considering them but nourishing and defending faith through them.
claims: Theology's end is nourishing and defending faith.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3057.summary: Replies to the second argument of the third set: theology orders its consideration of morals and believed things not to considering but to protecting the faith.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3068.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the fourth set of arguments.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3073.summary: Replies to the first argument of the fourth set: though theology treats speculable and practical matters perfectly, its end is not consideration but the defense of faith.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3086.summary: Replies to the Augustinian sapientia/scientia argument: theology is not properly science (an adhesive habit of conclusions) but wisdom as understanding of the noblest things, and it is still practical.
claims: Theology is wisdom, not science, and still practical.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3103.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the fifth set of arguments.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3108.summary: Replies to the affective arguments: a habit whose end is loving is practical, and so is one whose end is speculation, provided the speculation is directed, not elicited. The second argument falsely assumes charity is more useful but not nobler than understanding, to be discussed elsewhere.
claims: A habit whose end is love is practical.
Charity may be nobler than understanding (deferred).

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3130.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the contrary arguments.

ol96b1-bb9927-d1e3135.summary: Replies to the contrary arguments. Theology is not for its own sake but for the acts of faith and virtue. And it is false that no naturally acquired intellectual habit is ordered to love: moral science is, since virtues are loves (Augustine) or habitual choices (Aristotle), and moral science aims at choice ('we inquire to become good').
claims: Theology exists for the sake of faith and virtue, not for itself.
Moral science is ordered to love and choice.
